sentences.text: Vera, who had paced that turn four times and was twelve and had a notebook, said that it was not wrong.
"It's wrong," her grandmother said, "because you've got it going round the outside, and it went round the inside.
There was a chestnut there.
It went round the other side of the chestnut." "There's nothing there now." "No.
There's a stump six metres down under two hundred million litres of water, and you didn't see it, and neither did the eel." She turned the notebook.
"But it went round the inside.
I've walked that road four thousand times." And then she stopped, with her hand flat on the page, and did not say anything for a while.
Vera did not say anything either.
What her grandmother said, eventually, was: "I couldn't have told you that yesterday." She said that she had not been able to get the village back for about ten years.

That she could see the kitchen and she could see the front of the school and she could see two or three faces, and that everything in between had gone soft and would not come when she called it — and that this had frightened her more than she had told anybody, including Vera's mother, and that she had stopped trying because trying and failing was worse.
"And then you put a road in front of me," she said, "and I'm on it." They did the rest of it over that winter.

Vera would put a question — what's here, what's at the end of this, why does it turn — and her grandmother would be somewhere in 1962 and would answer it, and about a third of the time she would answer a question Vera had not asked, and Vera learned quickly to write those down and not interrupt.
The map they finished in March has one hundred and nine things on it.
Houses with names on them, which are the names of families and not of streets.
The two shops.
The place where the bus turned.
A well that is not on any official plan.
The chestnut, drawn as a circle, with the road going round the inside of it.
The reservoir filled that winter and the tower went under in January and has not been seen since.

Vera is twenty-eight and the map is in the parish office at Aldeia Nova, framed, next to the photographs, and there is a copy in the district archive because a woman from the archive came out and asked for one.
Her grandmother died in 2021.
The thing Vera says, when people ask her about it — and they do ask, because of the framed map, and because it is a good story about a drought and a fish — is that the eel did not know anything.
It was an eel in a pool.
Eels lie up in pools.

The pools were on the line of the road because the road was the low ground, and the road was the low ground because roads are built on ground you can walk on, and the whole of the mystery collapses the moment you look at it properly.
What the eel did was make her kneel down in the right place.

Everything else in that story was an old woman at a kitchen table who had been quietly losing something for ten years, and who got most of it back over one winter because a twelve-year-old asked her the questions in the right order — starting from the north, coming down the slope, going round the inside of the chestnut.
